caption:
Hit snooze again? 30 minutes is okay. Today's word: Snooze.

One Word No. 7. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: if you're someone who snoozes anyway and falls back asleep easily, a short snooze barely costs you sleep, and waking in stages may mean you're less likely to be pulled out of deep sleep.

THE RESEARCH: 31 regular snoozers slept in a sleep lab. One morning they snoozed for 30 minutes; another morning the first alarm got them up. Snoozing cost about 6 minutes of sleep, and on tests right after waking they did as well or a bit better. Mood, sleepiness and the morning stress hormone showed no clear change.

HOW:
1. Set the first alarm no more than 30 minutes before you have to be up.
2. Snooze if you like.
3. The last alarm means feet on the floor.

THE CATCH: it's one small lab study of people who already snooze, and only 30 minutes was tested. If you find it hard to fall back asleep, or you feel groggy all morning, one alarm at your real wake-up time is the simpler choice.

Do this: Snoozing anyway? Stop at 30 minutes, then get up.

Send this to whoever sets 5 alarms every morning.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #morningroutine #snooze #focus #oneword

caption:
Maths test coming up? Mix 3 kinds of problems in every practice set. It feels harder while you practise, and you remember more on the test.

WHY: when every problem on the page is the same kind, you know the method before you even read the question. On the real test the kinds are mixed, so the hard part is spotting which method each problem needs. Mixed practice trains exactly that.

HOW:
1. Pick 3 kinds of problems the test will cover (say, one from each of your last 3 chapters).
2. Take a few problems of each kind.
3. Put them in order 1 of each kind, then repeat: A, B, C, A, B, C.

THE RESEARCH: in a study by Rohrer and Taylor (University of South Florida), students learned to find the volume of 4 unusual shapes. While practising, the students who did one shape at a time scored 89% and the mixers 60%. A week later, on the test, it flipped: mixers 63%, one-at-a-time 20%. A 2019 review of 59 studies (Brunmair & Richter) found mixing helps on average, maths included.

THE CATCH: that experiment was small (18 students), and mixing feels worse while you do it, so expect more mistakes in practice. It helps when you have to tell kinds of problems apart (maths, science, question types). For learning lists of words, the same review found mixing did worse.

Do this tonight: 1 of each kind, then repeat. Take problems from your last 3 chapters and shuffle them into one set.

Send this to whoever has a maths test next week.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#studytips #studying #maths #exam #focus

Sources (checked Nov 3 2026):
1) Rohrer, D. & Taylor, K. (2007). The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning. Instructional Science, 35, 481–498. doi:10.1007/s11251-007-9015-8. Experiment 2: 18 undergraduates learned the volume of 4 obscure solids (wedge, spherical cone, spheroid, half cone) over 2 practice sessions a week apart. Practice scores: blocked 89%, mixed 60%. Test 1 week later: mixed 63%, blocked 20%. Authors: 'mixed practice produced superior test performance and inferior practice performance.' Checked on the paper (author PDF).
2) Brunmair, M. & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029–1052. doi:10.1037/bul0000209. 59 studies, 238 effect sizes: overall benefit of interleaving g = 0.42; mathematical tasks g = 0.34; words g = -0.39 (blocking did better). Checked on PubMed and the authors' manuscript.
Limits: one small experiment for the headline numbers; the review's effects vary by material.

caption:
Can't switch off? 45 minutes of calm music at bedtime, every night. In a 3-week study, calm music improved students' sleep. An audiobook didn't.

WHY: slow, quiet music gives a busy mind something easy to follow, without the story or words that keep you listening. Done every night, it also becomes a cue that it's time to sleep.

HOW:
1. Pick a calm playlist: slow, quiet, no lyrics you'll sing along to.
2. Volume low, phone face down out of reach.
3. Set a sleep timer for 45 minutes. On Spotify: tap ••• on the song, then Sleep timer, then 45 minutes.
4. Repeat every night for a few weeks.

THE RESEARCH: 94 students with poor sleep were split into 3 groups. One listened to calm classical music for 45 minutes at bedtime, one to an audiobook, one did nothing, every night for 3 weeks. Sleep quality improved only in the music group (Harmat, Takács & Bódizs 2008). A 2022 Cochrane review of 13 trials (1,007 adults with insomnia) found music probably improves how well people feel they sleep (moderate-certainty evidence).

THE CATCH: the improvement is in how people rated their sleep, and it builds over nights, not in one. Evidence that music makes you fall asleep faster is weaker (low certainty). If you've slept badly for weeks, talk to a doctor: insomnia has good treatments.

Do this tonight: Calm playlist on. Sleep timer: 45 minutes.

Send this to whoever is still scrolling at 1 am.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #insomnia #cantsleep #sleepbetter #focus

caption:
Bed at 11? Hard workout done by 10. Finish hard workouts 1 hour before bed. Evening exercise is fine for sleep; it's the hard session that ends right before bed that can keep you up.

Sleep tonight, Part 2. (Part 1, yesterday: lying awake? After about 20 minutes, get out of bed.)

WHY: a hard session leaves your heart rate and body temperature up for a while. Moderate exercise doesn't seem to do that enough to matter, and in the studies evening exercise slightly increased deep sleep.

HOW:
1. Pick your bedtime (say 11 pm).
2. Hard stuff (intervals, heavy lifting, a race-pace run) done by 10 pm.
3. The last hour: easy only. A walk, a stretch, a shower.

THE RESEARCH: a review of 23 studies (Stutz, Eiholzer & Spengler, ETH Zurich) found the studies 'do not support the hypothesis that evening exercise negatively affects sleep'. The authors' one caution: falling asleep, total sleep and sleep efficiency 'might be impaired after vigorous exercise ending ≤ 1 h before bedtime'.

THE CATCH: that caution rests on very little data (ETH's own summary says it was based on just one study), and the studies were in healthy adults. So it's a sensible buffer, not a hard law. If evening training clearly wrecks your sleep, move it earlier.

Do this tonight: Finish hard workouts 1 hour before bed. A walk or easy stretch later is fine.

Send this to whoever trains at 10:30 pm and then can't sleep.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #eveningworkout #fitness #sleepbetter #focus

Sources (checked Nov 2 2026):
1) Stutz, J., Eiholzer, R. & Spengler, C. M. (2019). Effects of Evening Exercise on Sleep in Healthy Participants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine, 49(2), 269–287. doi:10.1007/s40279-018-1015-0 (PMID 30374942). Abstract conclusions: 'The studies reviewed here do not support the hypothesis that evening exercise negatively affects sleep… sleep-onset latency, total sleep time, and SE might be impaired after vigorous exercise ending ≤ 1 h before bedtime.' Checked on the Springer article page.
2) ETH Zurich news release on the same review (EurekAlert!, Dec 2018): 23 studies met the quality requirements; deep sleep 21.2% after evening exercise vs 19.9% without; moderate exercise did not cause sleep problems in any study examined; the vigorous-exercise exception was based on just one study.
Limits: healthy adults, mostly lab studies; the 1-hour line is a caution, not a tested rule.
